2025.clinched: Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, 7 December 2025, final round (24 of 24)
2025.note: Norris clinched his first championship at the Abu Dhabi finale on 7 December 2025, where third place behind race winner Max Verstappen and teammate Oscar Piastri was exactly enough. It was the first time since the four-way shootout of 2010 that more than two drivers reached the last race still in contention, and the two-point verdict, 423 to 421, ended Verstappen's run of four straight titles. Norris took seven wins along the way and gave McLaren a drivers' champion for the first time since Lewis Hamilton in 2008.

2024.clinched: Las Vegas Grand Prix, 23 November 2024, two rounds to spare (round 22 of 24)
2024.note: Verstappen sealed his fourth consecutive title under the Las Vegas lights on 23 November 2024, finishing fifth, one place ahead of his only remaining rival Lando Norris, with Qatar and Abu Dhabi still to run. The decisive blow had come three weeks earlier at a rain-soaked Interlagos, where he won from 17th on the grid. He closed the year on 437 points to Norris's 374 with nine wins, even as Red Bull surrendered the constructors' championship to McLaren.

2023.clinched: Qatar Grand Prix sprint race, Lusail, Saturday 7 October 2023, with six grands prix still to run (round 17 of 22)
2023.note: Verstappen's third title arrived on a Saturday: second place in the sprint race at the Qatar Grand Prix on 7 October 2023 settled it with six grands prix still to run, making him the first driver to clinch a championship in a sprint. The season rewrote the record book, with 19 wins from 22 races, ten of them in a row between Miami and Monza, and a final margin of 290 points over teammate Sergio Pérez.

2022.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 9 October 2022, four rounds to spare (round 18 of 22)
2022.note: Verstappen retained the title by winning a rain-shortened Japanese Grand Prix at Suzuka on 9 October 2022, a race that ran only 29 of its 53 laps, and at first nobody was certain he was champion: the paddock expected reduced points until the FIA confirmed full points applied. Charles Leclerc's five-second penalty for cutting the final chicane dropped him to third and closed the arithmetic with four rounds to spare. Verstappen's 15 wins that year set a new single-season record, and he finished 146 points clear of Leclerc.

2021.clinched: Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, 12 December 2021, final round (22 of 22)
2021.note: The championship went to the last lap of the last race: at Abu Dhabi on 12 December 2021, a late safety car for Nicholas Latifi's crash let Verstappen pit for soft tyres and pass Lewis Hamilton at Turn 5 on the final lap. The two had arrived at the finale level on points after 21 rounds. Verstappen became the first Dutch world champion, 395.5 points to 387.5, in a decider whose safety-car handling stayed controversial long after the flag, while Mercedes still collected an eighth straight constructors' title.

2020.clinched: Turkish Grand Prix, Istanbul Park, 15 November 2020, three rounds to spare (round 14 of 17)
2020.note: Hamilton equalled Michael Schumacher's record of seven championships at the Turkish Grand Prix on 15 November 2020, winning from sixth on the grid on a treacherous wet Istanbul Park surface and taking the flag more than 30 seconds clear. He ran roughly 50 laps on a single set of intermediate tyres while his only remaining rival, teammate Valtteri Bottas, spun six times on the way to 14th. The title came with three races to spare in a season of 11 wins and 347 points.

2019.clinched: United States Grand Prix, Circuit of The Americas, 3 November 2019, two rounds to spare (round 19 of 21)
2019.note: Second place behind teammate Valtteri Bottas at the United States Grand Prix on 3 November 2019 made Hamilton a six-time champion with two rounds to spare; he had needed only eighth. A one-stop gamble nearly won him the race itself, and he held off Max Verstappen by under a second at the flag in Austin. The 413-point, 11-win season left only Schumacher's seven titles ahead of him.

2018.clinched: Mexican Grand Prix, Mexico City, 28 October 2018, two rounds to spare (round 19 of 21)
2018.note: Fourth place at the Mexican Grand Prix on 28 October 2018 was enough to make Hamilton a five-time champion, level with Juan Manuel Fangio, with two races to spare. Sebastian Vettel needed victory to stay alive and finished second to race winner Max Verstappen; his challenge had never recovered from Hockenheim in July, where he slid out of the lead in light rain while Hamilton won from 14th. The final accounting read 408 points to 320, with 11 wins for Hamilton.

2017.clinched: Mexican Grand Prix, Mexico City, 29 October 2017, two rounds to spare (round 18 of 20)
2017.note: Hamilton took his fourth title at the Mexican Grand Prix on 29 October 2017 in the strangest way of any of them: ninth place, after Vettel's front wing clipped his right-rear tyre on the opening lap and sent both contenders to the pits. Vettel recovered from 19th to fourth but needed second, so the crown was settled with Brazil and Abu Dhabi still to race. Hamilton finished the year 46 points clear, 363 to 317, with nine wins.

2016.clinched: Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, 27 November 2016, final round (21 of 21)
2016.note: Rosberg only had to survive the Abu Dhabi finale on 27 November 2016, and did, taking the second place he needed while race leader and teammate Hamilton deliberately slowed to back him into Vettel and Verstappen over the closing laps. The five-point margin, 385 to 380, settled an all-Mercedes title fight and made Nico and Keke Rosberg the second father-and-son champions after the Hills. Five days later Rosberg announced his retirement from the sport, still champion.

2015.clinched: United States Grand Prix, Circuit of The Americas, 25 October 2015, three rounds to spare (round 16 of 19)
2015.note: Hamilton clinched title number three by winning a wet-dry, safety-car-strewn United States Grand Prix in Austin on 25 October 2015, with three rounds to spare. The decisive moment came late, when Rosberg ran wide from the lead and Hamilton pounced for his tenth win of a season he closed out on 381 points to Rosberg's 322. It made him the first British driver to win back-to-back championships and matched his hero Ayrton Senna on three titles.

2014.clinched: Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, 23 November 2014, final round (19 of 19)
2014.note: The title was decided at Abu Dhabi on 23 November 2014, the only F1 race ever to award double points, and Hamilton removed the suspense by beating polesitter Rosberg off the line and winning outright. Rosberg's ERS failed on lap 25 and he limped home 14th, refusing the team's suggestion to retire the car. Hamilton's second title, six years after his first, came with 11 wins to Rosberg's five, 384 points to 317, and it gave Mercedes a first drivers' champion since Fangio in 1955.

2013.clinched: Indian Grand Prix, Buddh International Circuit, 27 October 2013, three rounds to spare (round 16 of 19)
2013.note: Vettel won the Indian Grand Prix on 27 October 2013 to take a fourth consecutive championship with three rounds to spare, then celebrated with doughnuts in front of the Buddh grandstands. He kept winning to the end: victories in Abu Dhabi, Austin and Brazil completed a run of nine straight wins to close the season, equalling Alberto Ascari's record streak. Thirteen wins and a 155-point margin over Fernando Alonso made it the most crushing of his four titles.

2012.clinched: Brazilian Grand Prix, Interlagos, 25 November 2012, final round (20 of 20)
2012.note: Vettel became the youngest triple champion at a chaotic, wet Interlagos finale on 25 November 2012 that he nearly lost at Turn 4 of the opening lap, where contact with Bruno Senna spun him to the back of the field with a damaged sidepod. He climbed back to sixth, which beat Fernando Alonso, second in the race, by three points, 281 to 278. It capped a season that had opened with seven different winners in the first seven races.

2011.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 9 October 2011, four rounds to spare (round 15 of 19)
2011.note: Needing a single point at Suzuka on 9 October 2011, Vettel finished third behind Jenson Button and Fernando Alonso and became, at 24, the youngest double world champion in the sport's history, with four races to spare. The defence was built on Saturdays as much as Sundays: 11 wins and a record 15 pole positions from 19 races, and a 122-point gap to runner-up Button by season's end.

2010.clinched: Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, 14 November 2010, final round (19 of 19)
2010.note: Vettel arrived at the Abu Dhabi finale on 14 November 2010 third in the standings, behind Alonso and Webber, in the first four-way title decider F1 had ever staged. He won from pole while Ferrari marked the wrong Red Bull, leaving Alonso and Webber stuck in midfield traffic behind Vitaly Petrov, and at 23 became the youngest world champion in the sport's history. The only time Vettel led the 2010 championship was after the chequered flag of its last race; the final margin over Alonso was four points, 256 to 252.

2009.clinched: Brazilian Grand Prix, Interlagos, 18 October 2009, one round to spare (round 16 of 17)
2009.note: Button clinched the title at Interlagos on 18 October 2009, storming from 14th on the grid to fifth with one round to spare while polesitter and closest pursuer Rubens Barrichello fell to eighth with a puncture. It completed the Brawn GP fairy tale: the team won both world championships in its only season of existence, the first constructors' crown ever taken by a debutant, with Button converting six wins from the first seven races into a 95-point total that held off Sebastian Vettel by 11.

2008.clinched: Brazilian Grand Prix, Interlagos, 2 November 2008, final round (18 of 18)
2008.note: Hamilton won his first title at Interlagos on 2 November 2008 by taking fifth place from Timo Glock at Juncao, the last corner of the last lap of the season, moments after a late shower had caught Glock out on dry tyres. Felipe Massa had won the race and was champion for around 20 seconds before the positions settled. The single-point margin, 98 to 97, made Hamilton, then 23, the youngest world champion yet, and the first British champion since Damon Hill in 1996.

2007.clinched: Brazilian Grand Prix, Interlagos, 21 October 2007, final round (17 of 17)
2007.note: Räikkönen began the final day of 2007 third in the championship, seven points behind Lewis Hamilton, and ended it champion by one, 110 to the 109 of both Hamilton and Fernando Alonso. Ferrari's pit sequencing at Interlagos on 21 October moved him ahead of teammate Felipe Massa for the win he had to have, while a gearbox glitch dropped Hamilton to seventh. It was the first time since 1986 that three drivers had taken a title fight into the season's last race.

2006.clinched: Brazilian Grand Prix, Interlagos, 22 October 2006, final round (18 of 18)
2006.note: Alonso completed back-to-back championships with second place behind Felipe Massa at Interlagos on 22 October 2006, the final round of an 18-race duel with Michael Schumacher. The contest had swung two weeks earlier at Suzuka, where Schumacher's engine let go while he led; needing only a point in Brazil, Alonso banked eight and won by 13, 134 to 121. The race doubled as Schumacher's farewell before his first retirement, and he signed off by climbing from a puncture back to fourth.

2005.clinched: Brazilian Grand Prix, Interlagos, 25 September 2005, two rounds to spare (round 17 of 19)
2005.note: Third place behind the McLarens of Juan Pablo Montoya and Kimi Räikkönen at Interlagos on 25 September 2005 made Alonso champion with two rounds to spare, and at 24 years and 59 days the youngest in the sport's history to that point. It ended Michael Schumacher's five-year reign and made him Spain's first Formula 1 world champion. Räikkönen also won seven races that year yet finished 21 points back, 133 to 112.

2004.clinched: Belgian Grand Prix, Spa-Francorchamps, 29 August 2004, four rounds to spare (round 14 of 18)
2004.note: Schumacher's seventh and final championship was sealed with second place behind Kimi Räikkönen at Spa on 29 August 2004, four rounds from the end, at the circuit where he had made his debut in 1991. He had won 12 of the season's first 13 races, missing only Monaco, and finished with 13 victories, a record at the time. Teammate Rubens Barrichello was the only driver still mathematically alive arriving in Belgium, and ended the year 34 points adrift, 148 to 114.

2003.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 12 October 2003, final round (16 of 16)
2003.note: Schumacher broke Fangio's 46-year-old record of five championships in the least Schumacher-like way imaginable: eighth place at the Suzuka finale on 12 October 2003, scraping the single point he needed after qualifying 14th in the wet and losing his front wing against Takuma Sato's BAR. Räikkönen, who needed to win with Schumacher scoreless, finished second to Rubens Barrichello and fell two points short, 93 to 91. No season in Ferrari's five-title run with Schumacher came closer to slipping away.

2002.clinched: French Grand Prix, Magny-Cours, 21 July 2002, six rounds to spare (round 11 of 17)
2002.note: No champion has ever finished the job earlier: Schumacher won at Magny-Cours on 21 July 2002, round 11 of 17, to claim the title in July with six races to spare, a record that still stands. The win came when Kimi Räikkönen slid on Allan McNish's oil with five laps left. Schumacher stood on the podium after every one of the season's 17 races, a feat no other driver has managed, winning 11 of them and finishing 67 points clear of teammate Rubens Barrichello.

2001.clinched: Hungarian Grand Prix, Hungaroring, 19 August 2001, four rounds to spare (round 13 of 17)
2001.note: Schumacher took his fourth championship by winning the Hungarian Grand Prix on 19 August 2001 from lights to flag, a victory that also equalled Alain Prost's all-time record of 51 wins on the same afternoon. The Ferrari one-two with Rubens Barrichello sealed the constructors' title as well, four rounds early, and made Schumacher the first back-to-back Ferrari champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953. His eventual margin over David Coulthard was 58 points, 123 to 65.

2000.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 8 October 2000, one round to spare (round 16 of 17)
2000.note: Schumacher ended Ferrari's 21-year wait for a drivers' champion, the first since Jody Scheckter in 1979, by beating Mika Häkkinen at Suzuka on 8 October 2000 with one round to spare. The pair traded the lead through the pit cycles until Schumacher stayed out three laps longer at the second stops, emerged in front, and controlled the run home. His third title, and first in red, closed at 108 points to Häkkinen's 89, with nine wins.

1999.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 31 October 1999, final round (16 of 16)
1999.note: Häkkinen settled the strangest title race of the era by winning the Suzuka finale outright on 31 October 1999, leading 50 of 53 laps after arriving four points behind Ferrari's Eddie Irvine; the final count was 76 to 74. His real rival had been missing for half the season: Michael Schumacher broke his leg in a brake-failure crash at Silverstone in July, leaving Irvine to carry Ferrari's challenge. Häkkinen went back-to-back even as Ferrari took the constructors' crown, their first since 1983.

1998.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 1 November 1998, final round (16 of 16)
1998.note: The 1998 decider at Suzuka on 1 November fell apart for Michael Schumacher before it began: he stalled from pole position at the second formation start and had to set off from the back of the grid, four points behind Häkkinen. He had charged back into podium contention when track debris left a slow puncture, and the tyre blew on lap 31 to end his race. Häkkinen led every lap for his eighth win of the season, sealing his first championship 100 points to 86 alongside McLaren's first constructors' title since 1991.

1997.clinched: European Grand Prix, Jerez, 26 October 1997, final round (17 of 17)
1997.note: Villeneuve took the 1997 title at the Jerez finale on 26 October, a weekend that began with the top three qualifiers setting an identical 1:21.072 and turned on lap 48, when championship leader Michael Schumacher steered into Villeneuve's Williams at the Dry Sack corner and bounced into the gravel himself. Villeneuve nursed his damaged car home in third place, enough for the crown in only his second season. In November the FIA excluded Schumacher from the championship classification altogether, which is why the records list Heinz-Harald Frentzen, 39 points back, as runner-up to Villeneuve's 81.

1996.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 13 October 1996, final round (16 of 16)
1996.note: Hill settled the all-Williams title fight by leading every one of the 52 laps at the Suzuka finale on 13 October 1996, his eighth win of the year, while teammate Jacques Villeneuve, nine points behind on arrival, lost a rear wheel on lap 37 and retired. Victory made him the first son of a world champion to take the title himself, 28 years after Graham Hill's second crown. It was also his last drive for Williams, and Hill called the win his leaving present to the team.

1995.clinched: Pacific Grand Prix, TI Circuit Aida, 22 October 1995, two rounds to spare (round 15 of 17)
1995.note: Schumacher won at Aida on 22 October 1995 to take his second title with two rounds still to run, the eighth victory of a season that would end with nine. At 26 he was the youngest double world champion in the sport's history to that point. Damon Hill was runner-up, 33 points back, and the same year gave Benetton its only constructors' championship. The race was a late addition to October: it had been scheduled for April, then moved after the Great Hanshin earthquake damaged the region's infrastructure.

1994.clinched: Australian Grand Prix, Adelaide, 13 November 1994, final round (16 of 16)
1994.note: The first of Schumacher's seven titles was settled by a collision. He arrived in Adelaide on 13 November 1994 a single point ahead of Damon Hill, and contact between the two put both out of the race, leaving the championship 92 to 91. It remains one of the most contested endings in the sport's history, and it made Schumacher the last Ford-powered drivers' champion.

1993.clinched: Portuguese Grand Prix, Estoril, 26 September 1993, two rounds to spare (round 14 of 16)
1993.note: Second place behind Michael Schumacher at Estoril on 26 September 1993 gave Prost his fourth championship with two rounds to spare, the first driver to reach four since Juan Manuel Fangio. He had missed the chance a race earlier at Monza, where his engine failed five laps from the end. Prost finished on 99 points to Ayrton Senna's 73. Prost had confirmed on the Friday of the Estoril weekend that he would retire, with Senna taking his Williams seat for 1994.

1992.clinched: Hungarian Grand Prix, Hungaroring, 16 August 1992, five rounds to spare (round 11 of 16)
1992.note: Mansell finished second behind Senna at the Hungaroring on 16 August 1992 and was champion with five races still to run, the earliest anyone had clinched the title at that point, a record that stood for a decade. He was 39 and in his twelfth season, and he had opened the year with five straight wins before adding three more. Nine victories across the season made him the first driver to win nine championship races in a single year. His team-mate Riccardo Patrese was runner-up.

1991.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 20 October 1991, one round to spare (round 15 of 16)
1991.note: Senna took his third and final championship at Suzuka on 20 October 1991, finishing second and waving Gerhard Berger through for the win as thanks for two seasons of support. His only mathematical rival, Nigel Mansell, had spun into a sand trap on lap 10 and retired. It was the fifth year in a row that the title was decided at Suzuka, and it made Senna the youngest three-time champion in the sport's history. The weekend is remembered as much for the press conference, where he finally spoke openly about the Suzuka collisions of 1989 and 1990.

1990.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 21 October 1990, one round to spare (round 15 of 16)
1990.note: Senna's second title was settled at the first corner on 21 October 1990, when he and Alain Prost collided and both retired on the spot, which was enough because Prost could no longer catch him with only Adelaide left. It was the exact reverse of 1989, when a collision between the same two drivers at the same circuit had handed Prost the championship. FIA president Jean-Marie Balestre called it a scandal that a title should be decided that way, and a year later, at the same track, Senna admitted he had gone into the corner determined not to yield.

1989.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 22 October 1989, one round to spare (round 15 of 16)
1989.note: Prost's third championship was confirmed in the stewards' room. He arrived at Suzuka on 22 October 1989 sixteen points clear of Ayrton Senna, who needed to win both remaining races. The two McLarens collided at the chicane on lap 47; Prost climbed out, while Senna had his front wing repaired and crossed the line first, only to be disqualified for rejoining the track incorrectly after a push start. Senna's licence was suspended for six months. It was Prost's last title with McLaren before he moved to Ferrari.

1988.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 30 October 1988, one round to spare (round 15 of 16)
1988.note: Senna's first championship came out of one of the worst starts of his career. He stalled from pole at Suzuka on 30 October 1988, bump-started the car on the slight downhill slope, and came back through the field to beat Prost by around thirteen seconds. The win was his eighth of the season, breaking the record of seven shared by Prost and Jim Clark. Had he not won, the title would have gone to Adelaide, where a Prost victory would have levelled the points and left Senna champion on race wins anyway.

1987.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Suzuka, 1 November 1987, decided before the race (round 15 of 16)
1987.note: Piquet took his third title without turning a wheel in the race. He arrived at the first Suzuka Grand Prix on 1 November 1987 twelve points ahead of his Williams team-mate Nigel Mansell, who crashed heavily in Friday qualifying at the Esses and suffered back injuries that ruled him out of both remaining rounds. That confirmed the championship for Piquet, who had won three races that year to Mansell's six. His own reaction was flat: he said he had not wanted it to end that way.

1986.clinched: Australian Grand Prix, Adelaide, 26 October 1986, final round (16 of 16)
1986.note: Three drivers could still take the title into Adelaide on 26 October 1986, and it turned on a tyre. Nigel Mansell needed third place and was running there when his left-rear exploded on the main straight with nineteen laps to go. Williams called Nelson Piquet in for a precautionary change, which handed Prost the lead and the race, and the championship finished Prost 72, Mansell 70, Piquet 69. Prost became the first driver to successfully defend the title since Jack Brabham in 1960, and Williams' internal fight cost them the drivers' crown in a year they won the constructors' by a distance.

1985.clinched: European Grand Prix, Brands Hatch, 6 October 1985, two rounds to spare (round 14 of 16)
1985.note: Fourth place at Brands Hatch on 6 October 1985 made Prost, at 30, the first French world champion, and he is still the only one. He had started sixth, dropped to 14th at the start and broken the lap record three times climbing back; his last rival, Michele Alboreto, was out on lap 13 with a blown turbo. Nigel Mansell won the race, the first victory of his career. Prost had lost the 1984 title by half a point to his own team-mate, which made this one the correction.

1984.clinched: Portuguese Grand Prix, Estoril, 21 October 1984, final round (16 of 16)
1984.note: The closest title-winning margin in the sport's history, and it still stands. Lauda needed second at Estoril on 21 October 1984 and got it when Nigel Mansell spun out of that position with 18 laps to go, a front-left brake problem ending his race. Alain Prost won the race, his seventh of the season, and lost the championship to his own team-mate by half a point, the half having been awarded at a rain-shortened Monaco. It was Lauda's third title, seven years after his second.

1983.clinched: South African Grand Prix, Kyalami, 15 October 1983, final round (15 of 15)
1983.note: Three drivers arrived at Kyalami on 15 October 1983 still able to win it. Piquet led from the start, and the championship was settled on lap 36 when Alain Prost climbed out of his Renault with a broken turbine. Told on the pit board that Prost was out, Piquet wound the boost down to be certain of finishing, dropped to third, and took the title 59 points to 57. It was the first championship won with a turbocharged engine and the last won by a Brabham driver. Renault sacked Prost after the race.

1982.clinched: Caesars Palace Grand Prix, Las Vegas, 25 September 1982, final round (16 of 16)
1982.note: Rosberg needed sixth place in the car park behind Caesars Palace on 25 September 1982 and finished fifth, taking the championship on 44 points to 39. He won only one race all year, at the Swiss Grand Prix, the first champion to manage it with a single victory since 1958. It was a season with no pattern to it at all: eleven different drivers won a race. Had John Watson won in Las Vegas and Rosberg scored nothing, Watson would have taken the title on a countback of wins.

1981.clinched: Caesars Palace Grand Prix, Las Vegas, 17 October 1981, final round
1981.note: Piquet won his first championship by a single point, 50 to 49, in a Las Vegas car park on 17 October 1981. Carlos Reutemann had arrived leading and started from pole, but his gearbox was failing by lap two and he finished eighth. Piquet, needing only to see the flag, faded to fifth in stifling heat on a new anticlockwise circuit that punished drivers' necks, and was so far gone by the end that mechanics had to lift him out of the car. Alan Jones won the race, the last of his Formula 1 career.

1980.clinched: Canadian Grand Prix, Circuit Ile Notre-Dame, Montreal, 28 September 1980, one round to spare (round 13 of 14)
1980.note: Jones and Nelson Piquet were separated by a single point when they arrived in Montreal on 28 September 1980, and they collided at the first corner, Piquet spinning into the wall and taking most of the field's running with him. The race was stopped and restarted; Piquet led it until his qualifying-specification engine failed on lap 24, and Jones won. It gave Williams its first drivers' championship and made Jones the second Australian champion after Jack Brabham.

1979.note: Scheckter won at Monza on 9 September 1979 half a second ahead of his team-mate Gilles Villeneuve, and the one-two took both championships for Ferrari in front of the tifosi. Villeneuve had agreed before the start to follow him home. Jacques Laffite, the only other man in contention, threw a valve on lap 42. Scheckter finished the year on 51 points to Villeneuve's 47, remains the only South African champion, and never won another Grand Prix. Ferrari would wait 21 years for its next drivers' title.

1978.clinched: Italian Grand Prix, Monza, 10 September 1978, two rounds to spare (round 14 of 16)
1978.note: Andretti became champion at Monza on 10 September 1978 and could not celebrate it. A chaotic start put ten cars into an accident from which James Hunt and Clay Regazzoni pulled his team-mate and title rival Ronnie Peterson clear of the flames; Peterson's leg injuries were not thought life-threatening, and he died the following day of an embolism. Andretti finished sixth in the restarted race after a jump-start penalty, and Peterson was awarded second in the championship posthumously. Andretti is still the last American world champion, and he later said he would trade the title to have his friend back.

1977.clinched: United States Grand Prix, Watkins Glen, 2 October 1977, two rounds to spare (round 15 of 17)
1977.note: Lauda needed one point at a wet Watkins Glen on 2 October 1977 and took four for fourth place, fourteen months after the Nurburgring crash that nearly killed him. James Hunt won the race and lost the championship. The second title was built on the reliability of the Ferrari 312 T2 rather than its speed: three wins, ten podiums, 72 points. Lauda then skipped the last two rounds and left for Brabham, having asked Enzo Ferrari for a raise and been refused.

1976.clinched: Japanese Grand Prix, Fuji Speedway, 24 October 1976, final round (16 of 16)
1976.note: Three points behind Lauda with one race left, Hunt took the title by one at Fuji on 24 October 1976. The race started in a downpour after 90 minutes of argument about whether it should run at all, and Lauda pulled into the pits after two laps and withdrew, saying afterwards that his life was worth more than a title. Hunt led, then lost places as the track dried, suffered a deflating tyre and pitted, and recovered to third, which was exactly enough. Mario Andretti won.

1975.clinched: Italian Grand Prix, Monza, 7 September 1975, one round to spare (round 13 of 14)
1975.note: Lauda needed half a point at Monza on 7 September 1975, the Canadian Grand Prix having been cancelled for lack of money, and third place behind his team-mate Clay Regazzoni gave him his first championship. Emerson Fittipaldi caught and passed him for second in the closing laps, which changed nothing. The same afternoon ended an eleven-year wait for a Ferrari constructors' title. Lauda's year was built on Mauro Forghieri's transverse-gearbox 312 T: five wins and nine poles from fourteen rounds.

1974.clinched: United States Grand Prix, Watkins Glen, 6 October 1974, final round (15 of 15)
1974.note: Fittipaldi and Clay Regazzoni arrived at Watkins Glen on 6 October 1974 level on points, so the title went to whichever finished ahead. Regazzoni's Ferrari had a broken damper that destroyed its tyres and he came home eleventh, four laps down, while Fittipaldi drove a careful fourth to take his second championship in three seasons on 55 points. It was McLaren's first constructors' title, by three points from Ferrari. The weekend was overshadowed by the death of Helmuth Koinigg, the second driver killed at the circuit in twelve months.

1973.clinched: Italian Grand Prix, Monza, 9 September 1973, two rounds to spare (round 13 of 15)
1973.note: Stewart needed one point at Monza on 9 September 1973 and had to earn it the hard way: a left-rear puncture on lap 8 dropped him to twentieth, a minute down. He came back through the field at around two seconds a lap faster than the cars ahead, reached fourth by lap 49, and set a new lap record for the chicaned circuit on the way. It was his third and final championship, and he announced his retirement three days later. Ronnie Peterson won the race.

1972.clinched: Italian Grand Prix, Monza, 10 September 1972, two rounds to spare (round 10 of 12)
1972.note: Fittipaldi won at Monza on 10 September 1972 to become the first Brazilian world champion and, at 25 years and 273 days, the youngest in the sport's history, a record that stood for 33 years until Fernando Alonso broke it in 2005. Jackie Stewart's challenge ended within a hundred metres of the start when his clutch failed. Fittipaldi was driving a spare Lotus 72D, his own car having been badly damaged in a transporter crash on the way to Monza, and said afterwards that he only realised he was champion the next morning, reading the papers.

1971.clinched: Austrian Grand Prix, Osterreichring, 15 August 1971, three rounds to spare (round 8 of 11)
1971.note: Stewart took his second title on a day he did not finish. A broken left-rear driveshaft ended his race at the Osterreichring on 15 August 1971, but Jacky Ickx retired with engine failure and Ronnie Peterson could only manage eighth, which left nobody able to catch him. He had won five of the first seven rounds and closed the year on 62 points. He remains the only driver crowned world champion in Austria. Jo Siffert won the race, and it was also the day Niki Lauda made his Formula 1 debut.

1970.clinched: United States Grand Prix, Watkins Glen, 4 October 1970, one round to spare (round 12 of 13)
1970.note: The only posthumous championship in the sport's history. Rindt was killed in practice at Monza on 5 September 1970 while leading the standings, and the title was mathematically settled at Watkins Glen on 4 October, where his replacement Emerson Fittipaldi won and Jacky Ickx, the only man who could still catch him, finished fourth. Rindt took it by five points. The trophy was presented to his widow, Nina. Ickx said later that he was glad he had never won the 1970 championship.

1969.clinched: Italian Grand Prix, Monza, 7 September 1969, three rounds to spare (round 8 of 11)
1969.note: Stewart had to win at Monza on 7 September 1969 to take the title there, and he won it by eight hundredths of a second. The lead changed fourteen times over 68 laps of slipstreaming, and the top four crossed the line covered by 0.19 seconds, Stewart ahead of Jochen Rindt with Jean-Pierre Beltoise and Bruce McLaren behind. He finished the season on 63 points with six wins, 26 clear of Jacky Ickx, and the year gave Matra its first and only constructors' championship.

1968.clinched: Mexican Grand Prix, Magdalena Mixhuca, 3 November 1968, final round (12 of 12)
1968.note: Three drivers could still win it in Mexico City on 3 November 1968: Hill on 39 points, Jackie Stewart on 36, Denny Hulme on 33. Hill led from the end of the opening lap and won the race, finishing the year on 48 points, twelve clear of Stewart, for his second championship. Lotus took the constructors' title the same afternoon. It closed a season the team had begun by losing Jim Clark at Hockenheim in April.

1967.clinched: Mexican Grand Prix, Magdalena Mixhuca, 22 October 1967, final round (11 of 11)
1967.note: For the first time in eight years two team-mates went to the last race able to win the championship. Hulme needed fourth place in Mexico City on 22 October 1967; Jack Brabham needed to win it with Hulme fifth or lower. Jim Clark won by over a minute despite having almost no clutch, Brabham was second and Hulme came home third a lap down, driving deliberately out of trouble. He is still the only New Zealander to have won the Formula 1 world championship, and the team had already taken the constructors' title three rounds earlier.

1966.note: Brabham clinched his third championship at Monza on 4 September 1966 from the side of the track. An oil leak stopped his BT19 on lap seven, and the title was his 24 laps later when John Surtees, the only man who could still catch him and needing to win all three remaining races, stopped with a fuel leak. He had won four of the previous six rounds. It remains the only time a driver has won the world championship in a car carrying his own name, and Brabham-Repco took the constructors' title too. Ludovico Scarfiotti won the race, the only Grand Prix victory of his career.

1965.clinched: German Grand Prix, Nurburgring, 1 August 1965, three rounds to spare (round 7 of 10)
1965.note: Clark took pole by more than three seconds, led every lap, set the fastest lap and won by sixteen seconds from Graham Hill, the only man who could still catch him. It was his sixth win of the season and his second championship, at 29. He had skipped Monaco that year to race at Indianapolis instead, where he led 190 of the 200 laps and won. He finished the season on 54 points, seven clear of Hill, and Lotus took the constructors' title the same afternoon.

1964.clinched: Mexican Grand Prix, Magdalena Mixhuca, 25 October 1964, final round
1964.note: The title changed hands three times in the last lap and a half. Three British drivers arrived in Mexico City on 25 October 1964 able to win it: Graham Hill on 39 points, Surtees on 34, Jim Clark on 30. Hill was delayed by a collision with Lorenzo Bandini, then Clark, leading comfortably, lost his engine near the end. That left Hill champion until Ferrari signalled Bandini to move over on the final lap, handing Surtees second place and the championship by a point, 40 to 39. Surtees, already a seven-time motorcycle world champion, remains the only man to have won world titles on two wheels and four.

1963.clinched: Italian Grand Prix, Monza, 8 September 1963, three rounds to spare (round 7 of 10)
1963.note: Clark won at Monza on 8 September 1963 and lapped the entire field bar the second-place car, taking his first championship with three rounds still to run, the first time anyone had settled it that early. He finished the year with seven wins from ten races and 73 points, 44 clear of Graham Hill, and because only the best six results counted he matched Alberto Ascari's feat of scoring every point available to him. The seven-win season record stood until Ayrton Senna won eight in 1988.

1962.clinched: South African Grand Prix, Prince George Circuit, East London, 29 December 1962, final round (9 of 9)
1962.note: Whoever won at East London on 29 December 1962 took the championship. Clark led from the first lap and was pulling clear when, on lap 61 of 82, his Lotus began spraying oil over the exhaust: a locking washer had not been fitted and a bolt had fallen out. Hill inherited the lead and was champion twenty laps later, his fourth win of the year giving him 42 points to Clark's 30. It was BRM's first manufacturers' title. Richie Ginther had given his team-mate his larger radiator for the race.

1961.clinched: Italian Grand Prix, Monza, 10 September 1961, one round to spare
1961.note: The bleakest championship in the sport's history. Hill and his Ferrari team-mate Wolfgang von Trips arrived at Monza on 10 September 1961 separated by four points. On the first lap von Trips and Jim Clark touched approaching the Parabolica; von Trips' car went into a spectator enclosure protected only by a waist-high fence, killing him and a number of spectators, the worst loss of life a championship race has seen. Hill won the race and the title by a single point, the first American world champion, and there was no celebration. Von Trips became the first driver awarded the runner-up place posthumously, Ferrari withdrew from the final round, and it was the last Grand Prix run on Monza's full ten-kilometre circuit with the banking.

1960.clinched: Portuguese Grand Prix, Boavista, Porto, 14 August 1960, two rounds to spare (round 8 of 10)
1960.note: Brabham's fifth win in a row, on the cobbles at Boavista on 14 August 1960, gave him a second championship with two rounds to spare. He took the lead on lap 36 when John Surtees went off with oil on his pedals, and Bruce McLaren followed him home for a Cooper one-two. He was the first driver since Alberto Ascari in 1953 to win consecutive titles, and the first to win a championship in a car he had helped design, the Cooper T53. Jim Clark scored the first podium of his career in third.

1959.clinched: United States Grand Prix, Sebring, 12 December 1959, final round
1959.note: Brabham pushed his Cooper to the line to become champion. Leading at Sebring on 12 December 1959 on a deliberately light fuel load, he ran dry 400 yards from the finish, waved his team-mate Bruce McLaren through for the first win of his career, climbed out and pushed the car up the hill to take fourth place, because the rules required him to finish unaided. It was the first title for an Australian, the first won in a rear-engined car, and the first for a British manufacturer, with Cooper taking the constructors' championship too. McLaren's victory made him the youngest Grand Prix winner at 22 years and 104 days.

1958.clinched: Moroccan Grand Prix, Ain-Diab, Casablanca, 19 October 1958, final round (11 of 11)
1958.note: Hawthorn became the first British world champion by a single point, and he did it finishing second. Stirling Moss needed to win at Ain-Diab on 19 October 1958 with fastest lap and Hawthorn outside the top three; Moss did his part, but Ferrari signalled Phil Hill to let Hawthorn through, which took him four laps to do, and the title was settled 42 to 41. It remains the only championship Grand Prix Morocco has hosted, and the weekend cost Vanwall's Stuart Lewis-Evans injuries from which he would not recover. Hawthorn retired days later and was killed in a road accident the following January, aged 29.

1957.clinched: German Grand Prix, Nurburgring, 4 August 1957, two rounds to spare (round 6 of 8)
1957.note: Fangio's fifth title came with the drive most often called the finest of his career. At 46, on softer Pirellis against the non-stopping Ferraris, he pitted for fuel and tyres, lost a minute to Mike Hawthorn and Peter Collins, and then broke the Nurburgring lap record on lap after lap to catch them both and win by 3.6 seconds. Five titles stood as the record until Michael Schumacher's sixth in 2003. It was Fangio's last Formula 1 victory and the last for Maserati as a constructor, and he said afterwards that he could not sleep for two nights.

1956.clinched: Italian Grand Prix, Monza, 2 September 1956, final round (8 of 8)
1956.note: Fangio's fourth championship was handed to him. His Ferrari's steering arm broke at Monza on 2 September 1956 while he led the standings by eight points from his team-mate Peter Collins and Maserati's Jean Behra, both of whom could still take the title. Ferrari asked Luigi Musso to give up his car and he refused in front of his home crowd; Collins, who could have won the championship himself, came in with fifteen laps to go and handed his over. Fangio finished second behind Stirling Moss, the shared points settled it, and Collins said he was 25 and had time. He was killed at the Nurburgring two years later.

1955.clinched: Italian Grand Prix, Monza, 11 September 1955, final round (7 of 7)
1955.note: Fangio won from pole at Monza on 11 September 1955 with Piero Taruffi seven tenths behind him for a Mercedes one-two, taking a third title and a second in a row on 40 points. The season had been cut to seven rounds: France was already gone and the German, Swiss and Spanish Grands Prix were all cancelled after the Le Mans disaster. It was the last Formula 1 win Mercedes would take before withdrawing from racing at the end of the year, and no Mercedes driver would be champion again until Lewis Hamilton in 2014. The race remains the only championship round ever run on Monza's combined road and banking circuit.

1954.clinched: Swiss Grand Prix, Bremgarten, 22 August 1954, two rounds to spare (round 7)
1954.note: Fangio won in the Bremgarten forest on 22 August 1954 by 57.8 seconds from Jose Froilan Gonzalez, lapping every car in the race except his, and the nine points made his best five scores unbeatable. He had begun the season at Maserati, winning in Argentina and Belgium, then moved to Mercedes and won in France and Germany, which makes him the only driver to have taken a championship driving for two teams in the same year. It was the last championship Grand Prix held in Switzerland: the country banned circuit racing after Le Mans the following summer, and the ban has largely stood ever since.

1953.clinched: Swiss Grand Prix, Bremgarten, 23 August 1953, one round to spare (round 8 of 9)
1953.note: Ascari needed only a top-five finish at Bremgarten on 23 August 1953 and won the race instead, fighting a gearbox problem and then engine trouble, pitting, rejoining behind his team-mates and ignoring instructions to hold position to pass them both for a Ferrari one-two-three. It made him the first driver to retain the championship. It was also his thirteenth Formula 1 win, all of them for Ferrari, and the last of his career. Accounts differ on exactly which round settled it: some place the clinch a race earlier at the Nurburgring, because only a driver's best four results counted.

1952.clinched: German Grand Prix, Nurburgring, 3 August 1952, two rounds to spare (round 6 of 8)
1952.note: Ascari won from pole at the Nurburgring on 3 August 1952, his fourth pole in a row, with Giuseppe Farina and Rudi Fischer completing a Ferrari one-two-three, and he set the fastest lap as well. He took six of the seven championship races he entered that season, having missed the Swiss Grand Prix because it clashed with Indianapolis 500 qualifying. Which round actually settled the title is contested: only the best four of eight results counted, so the arithmetic was complete well before the finale, while Ferrari's own history marks his sixth consecutive win, at Monza on 7 September, as the moment he became champion.

1951.clinched: Spanish Grand Prix, Pedralbes, 28 October 1951, final round (8 of 8)
1951.note: The first of Fangio's five titles was decided by wheel diameter. Ferrari had fitted smaller sixteen-inch rear wheels for the Pedralbes street circuit on 28 October 1951 and the tyres could not take the loading: Taruffi threw a tread on lap six, Villoresi on lap seven, Ascari on lap eight and Gonzalez on lap fourteen, and all of them lost time in the pits. Alfa Romeo had chosen eighteen-inch wheels. Fangio passed his team-mate Farina on lap three and Ascari on lap four, won comfortably and set the fastest lap; Ascari's fourth place was not enough. Alfa Romeo announced afterwards that it could not afford to compete in 1952.

1950.clinched: Italian Grand Prix, Monza, 3 September 1950, final round (7 of 7)
1950.note: Three Alfa Romeo team-mates went to Monza able to win the first world championship: Fangio on 26 points, Luigi Fagioli on 24 and Farina on 22, and only a Farina win would settle it in his favour. Fangio took pole but dropped a valve, and Farina won from third on the grid in a race only seven of the twenty-seven starters finished. Eight points took him to 30, ahead of Fangio on 26.5 and Fagioli on 24, an Alfa Romeo sweep of the standings. At 43, the Turin lawyer became the sport's first world champion, and he is still the only driver to have won the title in his home country.
